messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 76
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 73

# Case Vignette: Bernard

Bernard is a 76-year-old man of Dutch descent who has spent the better part of his adult life in the hospitality industry. He managed a series of mid-range hotels across Western Europe before settling into a senior management role at a large conference hotel in his adopted city, a position he held for nearly two decades before the incident that changed everything.

It happened on an otherwise unremarkable Tuesday morning seven years ago. A maintenance contractor, working without adequate supervision, accidentally ruptured a storage line connected to a commercial cleaning system in the hotel's basement. Bernard was the first manager on scene. He remembers the sharp, acrid smell before he understood what it was — a concentrated industrial solvent mixture that had begun venting into the lower corridor. He recalls trying to help two housekeeping staff out of the area before the fumes overwhelmed him. He was found collapsed near the service elevator and was hospitalized for eleven days with chemical burns to his airways and acute toxic injury to his lungs.

The physical recovery was slow and incomplete. Bernard was left with a persistent cough and reduced lung capacity, and his pulmonologist has been clear that some of that damage is permanent. But it is the interior damage — the kind that does not show on a scan — that now defines his days.

Bernard cannot enter a cleaning supply aisle in a supermarket without his chest tightening and his mind flooding with the image of the basement corridor, the yellowish haze hanging in the fluorescent light. He has learned to send his grocery order online. At the hotel where he still works part-time in an advisory capacity — a role his employer created partly out of loyalty, partly out of legal settlement — he avoids the maintenance corridors entirely. When the ventilation system kicks on and he catches an unusual smell, his body responds before his mind can catch up: his heart hammers, his hands go cold, and he finds himself pressing his back against the nearest wall, scanning for an exit. Colleagues have learned not to comment on it.

Sleep is where the worst of it lives. Bernard wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, sometimes mid-shout, sometimes simply rigid with dread, the dream always some variation of the same scene — the corridor, the smell, the moment his legs gave way. He lies awake afterward for hours, his mind cycling through what he should have done differently, whether he could have cleared the area faster, whether the two women he helped out remember that he hesitated for a moment before going back in.

He has been divorced for many years, and his two adult children live in different countries. He describes his social life in the careful, minimizing language of a man who has quietly withdrawn from most of it. He stopped attending the industry association dinners he once enjoyed. He cancelled a trip to visit his son in Canada twice, both times citing his health, though he acknowledges to himself that it was the thought of airports — the chemicals, the recycled air, the enclosed spaces — that stopped him. He describes feeling detached from people he used to feel close to, as though he is watching his own life from slightly outside it.

What troubles Bernard most, he says, is the sense that the person he was before that morning — competent, decisive, someone who ran toward problems rather than away from them — no longer exists. He managed hundreds of crises over his career. He was known for his steadiness. Now he startles at a smell, avoids a basement, and feels ashamed of both. He still goes to work because the hotel is the one place where his identity makes sense to him, even if he navigates it now like a man walking carefully around something broken on the floor.
